reviewerSummary: RFI 26-001 (CalVCB Compensation and Restitution System Modernization) is due 2026-09-24, 2:00 PM Pacific, via email to ITAcquisitions@victims.ca.gov. NOTE: this due date is already past relative to typical review cycles — confirm via Cal eProcure whether this RFI has been amended, reissued, or superseded before submitting [GAP-001]. The response must be the completed Attachment 1 worksheet itself, signed certification in Part I, 10 pages max, single-spaced, 12-point font, one-inch margins, no appendices or supplemental attachments. This draft is built to fit that worksheet structure with no cover material added. Fit is Partial overall: DataBillity's positioning depends heavily on facts not yet supplied — company size, founding date, platform architecture (home-grown vs. built on another platform), prior government implementations, and confirmed partner roster are all open. Without those, Part I (Company Information and Experience) and much of Part II/IV cannot be substantiated beyond placeholders. High-priority gaps, all owned by Prime: confirm RFI currency/amendment status [GAP-001]; supply company background, founding date, size, and structure [GAP-002]; confirm platform origin and whether home-grown or third-party-based [GAP-003]; list prior government implementations with agency names and applications [GAP-004]; resolve the two page-count/format ambiguities flagged for the issuer (whether Part I and question text count toward the 10-page limit, and whether any cover material is permitted at all) [GAP-005, GAP-006]; confirm CMMI/security certifications if claimed [GAP-011]; supply administrative identifiers (UEI, CAGE, NAICS, socioeconomic status) [GAP-018]. Medium/low gaps cover cost sizing assumptions, integration scope questions, and demonstration readiness. Decisions needed from the reviewer: whether to answer the nine-item upgrade/enhancement/configuration classification table now with placeholders or wait for product detail; whether to name partners in this RFI response at all given the 10-page ceiling. Recommend treating this as a market-shaping opportunity — the issuer explicitly asks for recommendations on the future solicitation (Part VI) and has not fixed solution architecture, hosting model, or transformation scope, which is where DataBillity's answer can have the most influence.
strategicNotes: This RFI is explicitly market research with no budget, timeline, or architecture preference fixed (R41, R59) — the highest-value contribution DataBillity can make is in Part VI (Evaluation/Recommendations), shaping how CalVCB frames the future solicitation around configurability rather than a specific product category. The ten challenge items (R5-R14) all trace back to one root cause CalVCB names implicitly: dependence on custom code for change. A response that repeatedly ties every answer back to 'configuration, not code' is likely to resonate more than a feature checklist. Watch for requirements that may be shaped around a specific incumbent or competitor: the emphasis on a rules-based auto-payment engine, attribute-level audit trails, and multilingual correspondence (items 2, 4, 5, 9) reads like functionality common to established GovTech claims platforms (e.g., established COTS players in state benefits/claims administration) — CalVCB's neutral framing (R41: 'no stated preference' among COTS, MOTS, integrated, or custom) is a genuine opening, but the specificity of the challenge list suggests CalVCB has already seen at least one vendor demo shape this list. Recommend the final response lean into recommendations that broaden evaluation criteria beyond any single architecture (e.g., recommending CalVCB score configurability-in-demo as heavily as feature checklists) to keep the field open rather than reinforce an existing frontrunner's narrative. No confirmed teaming partners exist in the current facts; capability gaps in specific platform certifications (GAP-011), accessibility conformance (GAP-009), and prior government implementation evidence (GAP-004) are candidates a systems-integrator or compliance-specialist partner could close if DataBillity decides to team before the future solicitation — this should be a decision made before, not during, final RFI drafting, since Part I explicitly asks about company experience and any partner named here becomes part of the public record (§1.I).
questions: Does the 10-page limit in Attachment 1 include the worksheet's own question text, Part I company information, and the signature block, or only the respondent's answers?

Section 1.F references written responses including the Attachment 1 worksheet, while Attachment 3 Q49 prohibits supplemental appendices or attachments; may respondents include a brief cover letter, and does it count toward the 10-page limit?
For Q48, should data cleansing and remediation be included in the base cost estimate or presented as an optional/separate line item?
Are exchanges with the Department of Justice, crime-reporting agencies, and courts in scope as required system integrations?
Is the external online application service intended to be replaced by the new solution, or integrated with it going forward?
Beyond the 350-400 internal, JP, and CRC users, how many external users (claimants, providers, advocates, court personnel) should respondents assume for capacity and licensing?
Is the September 24, 2026 response deadline still current, or has this RFI been amended, extended, or superseded by a later posting on Cal eProcure?

sections.title: Company Information and Experience
sections.body:
DataBillity (Billity AI) responds to this RFI as Prime. Our company background, including size, founding date, and corporate structure, is [GAP-002 | Prime | Confirm company founding date, size, and structure for Part I narrative]. We are not able to state a specific founding year, employee count, or revenue figure in this draft because those facts were not provided; the final submission must include this information as requested (Att. 1 Part I) rather than leave it blank, since the worksheet itself is the entire response and no supplemental company profile may be attached (Att. 3 Q49).

Our platform, DataBillity, is built to support configurable claims, compensation, and benefits administration workflows for government programs. Whether the platform is home-grown or built on a third-party base, and the specific version/architecture in use, is [GAP-003 | Prime | Confirm platform origin: home-grown vs. built on another organization's base, and current version]. This detail is required directly by the worksheet (Att. 1 Part I) and also underpins our answers on scalability and upgrade cadence in Part II and Part IV, so it should be resolved before final submission.

Our experience implementing this or a related solution with other government agencies, including specific department names and the applications implemented, is [GAP-004 | Prime | Supply list of prior government implementations: agency names, applications, dates, outcomes]. We will not cite specific client names, contract numbers, or outcome metrics that are not confirmed in our records, consistent with the requirement to avoid unverifiable claims in a response that becomes a public record (§1.I). Once confirmed, this experience should be summarized here with agency name, application/module implemented, approximate size (users or claim volume), and relevance to CalVCB's claims-and-restitution lifecycle (intake, eligibility, bill review, appeals, adjustments, correspondence), since that is the strongest evidence CalVCB can use to gauge fit.

Administrative identifiers required for a complete Part I certification and any subsequent teaming record — UEI, CAGE code, NAICS code(s), business size, and socioeconomic status — are [GAP-018 | Prime | Supply UEI, CAGE, NAICS code(s), business size, and socioeconomic status for certification]. These must be confirmed and entered before the signed certification required in Part I can be executed (Att. 1 instructions).

If DataBillity intends to name confirmed subcontractors or partners in this response, each partner's administrative information (legal name, address, identifiers, size/socioeconomic status, NAICS, contract vehicles, and point of contact) must also be supplied; no partners are confirmed in the facts available for this draft, so no partner-specific experience or identifiers are cited here. Given the 10-page ceiling and the prohibition on supplemental attachments (Att. 3 Q49), we recommend limiting Part I to Prime-company information plus, if space allows, a single-line summary of any confirmed partner's role — full partner qualification detail would need to compete for the same page budget as the technical answers in Parts II through VI.

sections.title: Solution
sections.body:
Our proposed solution is a configurable claims, compensation, and restitution platform intended to replace the custom-coded functionality in CaRes with rules-driven, no-code/low-code workflows, directly addressing the ten challenge items CalVCB describes (§1.D items 1-10). Specifically: (1) workflow, correspondence, and reporting changes would be handled through configuration rather than custom code, addressing the agility gap in challenge items 1, 4, and 10 (R42); (2) an adjustments module would track returned payments against lifetime limits without requiring code changes or reliance on external databases, addressing item 2; (3) a configurable appeals workflow would replace the current externally tracked, manually integrated process, addressing item 3; (4) a correspondence engine would generate letters from templates rather than hard-coded logic, with support for languages beyond English and Spanish subject to confirming the full required language list, addressing item 4; (5) an attribute-level audit trail would record who took what action at each phase, addressing item 5; (6) provider information would be integrated with claim records rather than held separately, addressing item 8; and (7) system-enforced separation-of-duties warnings and notifications would replace manual controls, addressing item 9.

Whether the online application intake (item 6) is replaced outright or integrated with the new system of record depends on CalVCB's intent, which the RFI itself leaves open [GAP-007 | Prime | Confirm with issuer whether external online application service is to be replaced or integrated — see Questions for Issuer]; our approach supports either path, since intake can be configured as a native module or as an integration point.

The specific products and modules that make up our proposed solution — including which are used off-the-shelf, which require configuration, and which would require custom development to meet CalVCB's challenge statement — are [GAP-008 | Prime | Confirm product/module list and classify each as off-the-shelf, configured, or customized for CalVCB's ten challenge items]. We are not able to state definitive module names or off-the-shelf/configured/customized status without this confirmation, and we flag this as a capability-scoping gap rather than assume coverage we cannot verify.

On scalability and flexibility: our typical approach is to build on a platform architecture that separates configuration (workflows, rules, letters, reports) from code, so that future changes in security, accessibility, or compliance requirements — for example, evolving NIST 800-53 controls, accessibility standards, or new SIMM/SAM policy on GenAI use (R57) — can be accommodated through configuration and platform upgrades rather than custom rework. This design pattern also supports the 350-400 role-based users across CalVCB headquarters and county JP and CRC offices (R30) without architectural change, since role-based configuration is intended to scale by adding roles and permissions rather than new code paths. Confirmation of our platform's specific accessibility conformance level (e.g., WCAG version) is [GAP-009 | Prime | Confirm accessibility conformance standard and version supported by the platform].

sections.title: Integration (Inputs and Outputs)
sections.body:
Our platform is intended to support integration with the systems CalVCB has identified as in scope: the existing Bill Review Service, the State Controller's Office, the Franchise Tax Board, EDD, and TotalAgility (R53, R79). Our typical approach to integration uses standard, documented APIs and file-based exchange methods appropriate to each partner system's own interface capabilities; the specific integration method (API, secure file transfer, or middleware) for each of these five systems has not been confirmed against our platform's current connector library, so this is [GAP-010 | Prime | Confirm specific integration method — API, SFTP, or middleware — for Bill Review Service, SCO, FTB, EDD, and TotalAgility].

On the bill-adjudication interface specifically, the RFI states the solution must at minimum support the existing interface, with integrated adjudication open for consideration (R54). We would propose supporting the existing interface as the baseline and treating a more tightly integrated adjudication workflow as a configuration option to be scoped once CalVCB's adjudication rules and auto-payment logic are documented in detail.

We note that the RFI's own Q&A leaves open whether exchanges with the Department of Justice, crime-reporting agencies, and courts are in scope as required integrations, since the narrative describes these exchanges as part of eligibility determination but the Q&A integration list omits them (R96). We recommend CalVCB clarify this before a future solicitation is issued, since it materially affects integration scope and cost — see Questions for the Issuer.

Input/output capabilities of our platform, including supported file formats, batch versus real-time exchange, and reporting export formats (e.g., replacing the current SSRS/Power BI reporting stack, R83), are described only generally here because specific technical specifications (API standards supported, data formats, throughput limits) are [GAP-012 | Prime | Confirm specific I/O technical specifications: supported API standards, file formats, batch/real-time capability, and reporting export formats]. Our typical approach is to expose configurable report builders and standard export formats (e.g., CSV, PDF) alongside role-based dashboards, intended to reduce the current dependency on custom SSRS/Power BI development for report changes (item 10).

sections.title: Approach
sections.body:
Implementation methodology and timeline: Our typical approach to a modernization of this scope is a phased implementation beginning with business process discovery and requirements confirmation, followed by iterative configuration, integration build-out, data migration, and user acceptance testing, then phased or full cutover depending on CalVCB's risk tolerance. Because no budget, funding range, or implementation timeline has been established for this effort (R59, R90), we do not commit to a specific duration here; a representative timeline based on comparable implementations is [GAP-013 | Prime | Provide representative implementation timeline example from a comparable engagement within the last 5 years, per R108]. We recommend CalVCB consider a phased rollout — for example, HQ headquarters functions first, followed by county JP and CRC office rollout — to manage the 350-400 role-based user transition (R30), though a single-cutover approach remains viable and the RFI does not state a preference (R41).

Business-understanding approach: our typical approach begins with structured discovery sessions mapped to CalVCB's stated challenge themes — agility and change cost, missing functions and workarounds, controls and audit, and usability/accessibility (R42-R45) — to validate root causes before configuration begins, rather than assuming the ten listed challenge items are exhaustive.

User acceptance testing: our typical approach uses role-based UAT scripts tied to each workflow (intake, eligibility, emergency awards, bill review, appeals, adjustments, restitution/offender tracking, correspondence), executed by CalVCB HQ, JP, and CRC representatives before cutover, with defect triage and resolution cycles prior to sign-off.

Data validation and migration: our typical approach validates source data in CaRes against target data models before migration, using reconciliation reports to confirm record counts, claim status, and document completeness match between source and target. Migration scope, per the RFI, is active claims with full history and supporting documents; external databases are explicitly excluded (R58). Specific record counts and historical data volumes are not available to us; the RFI itself directs respondents to CalVCB's Annual Report for these figures (R88), so our cost and effort estimates in Part V are stated as planning-level assumptions pending that data [GAP-014 | Prime | Pull record counts, claim/bill/payment volumes, and historical data years from CalVCB Annual Report before finalizing migration approach and cost]. Whether data migration is included in the base cost or billed separately is addressed in Part V.

Upgrades, enhancements, and configuration changes: our typical approach defines a system/platform upgrade as a vendor-released change to the core platform (e.g., security patch, version release) that CalVCB does not need to fund individually; an enhancement as a new capability added to the platform roadmap, potentially available to all customers; and a configuration change as a CalVCB-specific adjustment to workflows, rules, letters, or reports made within the existing platform without code changes. Our specific upgrade release cadence and enhancement schedule are [GAP-015 | Prime | Confirm platform upgrade release frequency and enhancement release schedule]. Classification of the nine sample functional change items referenced in Attachment 1 against these three categories requires the actual item list, which is not included in the facts available for this draft: [GAP-016 | Prime | Obtain the nine sample functional change items from Attachment 1 and classify each as System Upgrade, Enhancement, or Configuration].

IT technical and functional support: our typical approach provides tiered support — technical support for platform/infrastructure issues and functional support for workflow/configuration questions — with defined service levels. Specific support tiers, hours, and response-time commitments applicable to this engagement are [GAP-017 | Prime | Confirm support tier structure, hours of coverage, and response-time targets to state as our typical approach, not a binding commitment].

Security and compliance: CalVCB requires compliance with NIST 800-53, FISMA, and SAM 5300, with no CJIS or IRS 1075 requirement (R56), and any GenAI use must follow SIMM 5305-F and SAM 5300 (R57). Whether our platform currently meets or maps to these specific standards, including any independent assessment or authorization status, is [GAP-011 | Prime | Confirm platform's current compliance posture and any certifications/assessments against NIST 800-53, FISMA, and SAM 5300]. We would not propose GenAI features for this engagement unless and until governance under SIMM 5305-F is scoped with CalVCB.

sections.title: Costing Model
sections.body:
No budget, funding range, or implementation timeline has been established by CalVCB for this effort (R59, R90), and the RFI requests a non-binding cost model for planning purposes only, broken down by one-time versus recurring cost, module, and phase (R60). Consistent with that instruction, any figures in our final submission would be labeled explicitly as a rough order of magnitude (ROM), not a quote or offer, and tied to stated sizing assumptions (350-400 internal/county role-based users, per R30; external user volume unconfirmed, per R98).

We are not able to provide dollar figures in this draft because no pricing inputs were supplied in the grounding facts available to us: [GAP-019 | Prime | Supply ROM cost inputs for implementation, product/license, maintenance, support, and training, broken down by one-time vs. recurring and by phase, explicitly labeled non-binding]. Once supplied, the cost model should be organized by: (1) one-time implementation costs (discovery, configuration, integration build, data migration, testing, training/OCM); (2) recurring costs (licensing/subscription, maintenance, ongoing support); and (3) module-level breakdown aligned to the functional areas in Part II (intake, eligibility, bill review, appeals, adjustments, correspondence, reporting).

On data migration cost treatment specifically: whether migration effort is included in base implementation cost or billed as a separate line item is [GAP-020 | Prime | Decide and state whether data migration is included in base cost or billed separately, consistent with R113]. We recommend stating this explicitly either way, since the RFI's own Q&A left this ambiguous for CalVCB as well (R95) — see Questions for the Issuer.

All cost figures in the final submission would carry the sizing-assumption caveat required by §1.F: assumptions about user counts, data volumes, and integration count materially affect the estimate, and actual pricing would depend on requirements confirmed during a future, more detailed procurement.

sections.title: Evaluation
sections.body:
CalVCB has not yet decided the solution approach (COTS, MOTS, integrated product set, COTS Configurable, or custom), phased versus single cutover, or whether this effort remains a technology replacement versus a broader business transformation (R41). We recommend CalVCB use the upcoming invite-only demonstrations (R61) to evaluate configurability directly — specifically, ask each vendor to demonstrate making a workflow, correspondence template, or report change live, without code, since the ten challenge items are fundamentally about configuration agility (R42-R45) rather than any single missing feature. We also recommend CalVCB establish demonstration success criteria before October 2026, since none currently exist (R91); criteria tied to the nine challenge-item categories (adjustments, appeals, correspondence, audit trail, separation of duties, reporting) would let CalVCB score vendors consistently.

On scope, we recommend CalVCB resolve, before the future solicitation is issued, whether the external online application service is to be replaced or integrated (R97), whether DOJ/crime-reporting/court exchanges are in-scope integrations (R96), and what external user volume (claimants, providers, advocates, court personnel) should be assumed for licensing and capacity planning beyond the 350-400 internal/county users (R98) — each of these affects both technical architecture and cost estimates materially enough that leaving them open in a future RFP would produce inconsistent vendor responses.

On cost comparability, we recommend the future solicitation specify whether data cleansing/remediation should be priced in the base estimate or as an optional line item (R95), so that vendor cost models can be compared on equal terms.

Regarding the solution demonstration itself (§1.G), our readiness and specific demonstration content would depend on confirmation of the module/product scope in Part II: [GAP-021 | Prime | Prepare demonstration scenarios once product/module scope is confirmed and CalVCB issues demonstration success criteria].
